questions.question: Let f(x) be a polynomial and g(x) = f'(x) be its derivative. If the degree of (f(x)+ f(-x)) is 10, then the degree of (g(x)-g(-x)) is ________.
questions.explanation:
[latex]f(x)+f(-x)[/latex] keeps only the even powers of f (times 2). Its degree is 10, so f has an [latex]x^{10}[/latex] term (and no higher even power).

[latex]g(x)-g(-x)[/latex] keeps only the odd powers of g = f'. Even powers of f become odd powers of g: [latex]x^{10}\rightarrow10x^9[/latex] is the highest.

Degree = 9

Answer: 9

questions.question: Consider [latex]4 \times 4[/latex] matrices with their elements from [latex]\{\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{1}\}[/latex]. The number of such matrices with even number of [latex]\mathbf{1}[/latex] s in every row and every column is
questions.explanation:
We need [latex]4\times4[/latex] binary matrices where every row and every column has an even number of [latex]1[/latex]s.

Freely choose the top-left [latex]3\times3[/latex] sub-block: this can be filled in any of [latex]2^{9}=512[/latex] ways.

Once this [latex]3\times3[/latex] block is fixed, the entries in the [latex]4[/latex]th column (for the first [latex]3[/latex] rows) are forced so that each of those rows has an even number of [latex]1[/latex]s, and similarly the entries in the [latex]4[/latex]th row (for the first [latex]3[/latex] columns) are forced by the column parity condition. The single remaining corner entry (row [latex]4[/latex], column [latex]4[/latex]) is then also forced, and it is easy to check the row-[latex]4[/latex] parity and column-[latex]4[/latex] parity conditions become consistent automatically.

So the count of valid matrices [latex]=2^{(4-1)^2}=2^9=512[/latex].

Answer: 512

questions.question:
Consider the given function [latex]f(x)[/latex].

[latex]f(x) = \begin{cases} ax + b & \text{for } x < 1 \\ x^3 + x^2 + 1 & \text{for } x \geq 1 \end{cases}[/latex]

If the function is differentiable everywhere, the value of [latex]b[/latex] must be ________. (rounded off to one decimal place)
questions.explanation:
For [latex]f[/latex] to be differentiable at [latex]x=1[/latex], it must first be continuous there, and then have matching one-sided derivatives.

Continuity: left-hand value [latex]=a(1)+b=a+b[/latex]; right-hand value [latex]=1^3+1^2+1=3[/latex]. So [latex]a+b=3[/latex].

Matching derivatives: left derivative [latex]=\dfrac{d}{dx}(ax+b)=a[/latex]. Right derivative [latex]=\dfrac{d}{dx}(x^3+x^2+1)=3x^2+2x[/latex], evaluated at [latex]x=1[/latex]: [latex]3+2=5[/latex]. So [latex]a=5[/latex].

Substituting back: [latex]b=3-a=3-5=-2[/latex].

Answer: -2.0

questions.question:
Consider the following two statements with respect to the matrices [latex]A_{m \times n},B_{n \times m},C_{n \times n} \text{ and }D_{n \times n},[/latex]

Statement 1: [latex]tr(AB) = tr(BA)[/latex]
Statement 2: [latex]tr(CD) = tr(DC)[/latex]

where[latex]tr()[/latex] represents the trace of a matrix. Which one of the following holds?

options.A: Statement 1 is correct and Statement 2 is wrong.
options.B: Statement 1 is wrong and Statement 2 is correct.
options.C: Both Statement 1 and Statement 2 are correct.
options.D: Both Statement 1 and Statement 2 are wrong.

questions.explanation:
[latex]tr(AB)=\sum_i\sum_k a_{ik}b_{ki}=\sum_k\sum_i b_{ki}a_{ik}=tr(BA)[/latex]. This holds for any [latex]A_{m\times n}[/latex], [latex]B_{n\times m}[/latex] (AB is [latex]m\times m[/latex], BA is [latex]n\times n[/latex]).

Statement 2 is the special case of square matrices, so it is also true.

Answer: Both Statement 1 and Statement 2 are correct

questions.question: For a real number [latex]a[/latex], let [latex]I(a)=\int_{-1}^{1}\left(3 x^{2}-a x+1\right) d x[/latex]. Which of the following statements is/are true?

options.A: The value of [latex]I(a)[/latex] is independent of the value of [latex]a[/latex]
options.B: The value of [latex]I(a)[/latex] can vary with the value of [latex]a[/latex]
options.C: There exists [latex]a \in(-\infty,+\infty)[/latex] such that [latex]I(a)[/latex] is a positive real number
options.D: There exists [latex]a \in(-\infty,+\infty)[/latex] such that [latex]I(a)[/latex] is a negative real number

questions.explanation:
[latex]I(a)=\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{1}(3x^2-ax+1)\,dx[/latex]

The middle term [latex]-ax[/latex] is an odd function of [latex]x[/latex], so its integral over the symmetric interval [latex][-1,1][/latex] is exactly [latex]0[/latex], regardless of the value of [latex]a[/latex]. Only the even part survives:
[latex]I(a)=\displaystyle\int_{-1}^1(3x^2+1)\,dx=\Big[x^3+x\Big]_{-1}^{1}=(1+1)-(-1-1)=2-(-2)=4[/latex]

So [latex]I(a)=4[/latex] for every real [latex]a[/latex] — the value is completely independent of [latex]a[/latex]. Since it's always [latex]4>0[/latex], there certainly exists (in fact, every) [latex]a[/latex] for which [latex]I(a)[/latex] is a positive real number; but there is no [latex]a[/latex] making it negative, and the value does not "vary."

Answer: I(a) is independent of a; and there exists a for which I(a) is positive (true for every a, since I(a)=4 always).

questions.question:
Which one of the following statements is TRUE about every n x n matrix with only real
eigenvalues?

options.A: If the trace of the matrix is positive and the determinant of the matrix is negative, at least one of its eigenvalues is negative.
options.B: If the trace of the matrix is positive, all its eigenvalues are positive.
options.C: If the determinant of the matrix is positive, all its eigenvalues are positive.
options.D: If the product of the trace and determinant of the matrix is positive, all its eigenvalues are positive.

questions.explanation:
Trace = sum of eigenvalues, determinant = product of eigenvalues.

- If det [latex]\lt[/latex] 0, the product is negative, so at least one eigenvalue is negative [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] option 1 true.
- Counter-examples for others: eigenvalues 3, [latex]-[/latex]1 (trace [latex]\gt[/latex] 0); [latex]-[/latex]1, [latex]-[/latex]2 (det [latex]\gt[/latex] 0); [latex]-[/latex]1, [latex]-[/latex]1, 5 (trace and det both positive).

Answer: If trace is positive and determinant is negative, at least one eigenvalue is negative

questions.question: Let [latex] x [/latex] and [latex] y [/latex] be random variables, not necessarily independent, that take real values in the interval [latex] [0,1] [/latex]. Let [latex] z=x y [/latex] and let the mean values of [latex] x, y, z [/latex] be [latex] \bar{x}, \bar{y}, \bar{z} [/latex], respectively. Which one of the following statements is TRUE?
questions.explanation:
Since [latex]0\le y\le1[/latex], we always have [latex]z=xy\le x[/latex]. Taking means: [latex]\bar z\le\bar x[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] always TRUE.

Others depend on how x and y are related:
- [latex]y=x[/latex] uniform on [0, 1]: [latex]\bar z=E[x^2]=\frac13 \gt \frac14=\bar x\bar y[/latex] (so = and [latex]\le[/latex] fail).
- [latex]y=1-x[/latex]: [latex]\bar z=\frac12-\frac13=\frac16 \lt \frac14[/latex] (so [latex]\ge[/latex] fails).

Answer: [latex]\bar z\le\bar x[/latex]

questions.question:
Consider the following matrix:
[latex]\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 4 & 8\\ 1& 3 & 9 &27 \\ 1 & 4 & 16 &64 \\ 1 & 5 & 25 &125 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
The absolute value of the product of Eigenvalues of R is _________ .

Answer: 12

questions.question: The value of the expression [latex]13^{99}[/latex](mod 17), in the range 0 to 16, is _________.
questions.explanation:
[latex]13\equiv-4\pmod{17}[/latex], so [latex]13^2\equiv16\equiv-1[/latex] and [latex]13^4\equiv1[/latex].

[latex]99=4\times24+3\Rightarrow13^{99}\equiv13^3=13^2\cdot13\equiv-13\equiv4\pmod{17}[/latex]

Answer: 4

Using Doolittle LU (unit diagonal in L):
- Row 1 of U = [1, 1, [latex]-[/latex]2]; [latex]L_{21}=1,\ L_{31}=2[/latex]
- [latex]U_{22}=3-1=2,\ U_{23}=-1-(-2)=1[/latex]
- [latex]L_{32}=\frac{1-2\cdot1}{2}=-\frac12[/latex]
- [latex]U_{33}=-5-2(-2)-(-\frac12)(1)=-\frac12[/latex]

Solving the system: eq2 [latex]-[/latex] eq1 gives [latex]2x_2+x_3=3[/latex]; eq3 [latex]-[/latex] 2[latex]\cdot[/latex]eq1 gives [latex]x_2+x_3=1[/latex]. So [latex]x_2=2,\ x_3=-1,\ x_1=4-2-2=0[/latex].

Answer: [latex]L_{32}=-\frac12,\ U_{33}=-\frac12,\ x_1=0[/latex]

questions.question:
Consider a system of linear equations [latex]P X = Q [/latex] where [latex]P \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} [/latex] and [latex]Q \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 1} [/latex]. Suppose [latex]P [/latex] has an [latex]LU [/latex] decomposition, [latex]P = LU [/latex], where

[latex] L = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ l_{21} & 1 & 0 \\ l_{31} & l_{32} & 1 \end{bmatrix} \quad \text{and} \quad U = \begin{bmatrix} u_{11} & u_{12} & u_{13} \\ 0 & u_{22} & u_{23} \\ 0 & 0 & u_{33} \end{bmatrix} [/latex]

Which of the following statement(s) is/are TRUE?

options.A: The system [latex]P X = Q [/latex] can be solved by first solving [latex]L Y = Q [/latex] and then [latex]U X = Y [/latex].
options.B: If [latex]P [/latex] is invertible, then both [latex]L [/latex] and [latex]U [/latex] are invertible.
options.C: If [latex]P [/latex] is singular, then at least one of the diagonal elements of [latex]U [/latex] is zero.
options.D: If [latex]P [/latex] is symmetric, then both [latex]L [/latex] and [latex]U [/latex] are symmetric.

questions.explanation:
Solving via [latex]LY=Q[/latex] then [latex]UX=Y[/latex]: substituting [latex]P=LU[/latex] into [latex]PX=Q[/latex] gives [latex]L(UX)=Q[/latex]; setting [latex]Y=UX[/latex], we solve [latex]LY=Q[/latex] first (easy, forward substitution since [latex]L[/latex] is lower triangular), then [latex]UX=Y[/latex] (easy, back substitution). True — this is exactly the standard LU-solve method.

If [latex]P[/latex] is invertible, both [latex]L,U[/latex] invertible: [latex]L[/latex] is unit lower-triangular (diagonal all [latex]1[/latex]s), so [latex]\det(L)=1[/latex] always, regardless of [latex]P[/latex] — [latex]L[/latex] is always invertible. Since [latex]\det(P)=\det(L)\det(U)=\det(U)[/latex], if [latex]P[/latex] is invertible ([latex]\det(P)\ne0[/latex]) then [latex]\det(U)\ne0[/latex] too. True.

If [latex]P[/latex] singular, some diagonal element of [latex]U[/latex] is zero: since [latex]\det(P)=\det(U)[/latex] (product of [latex]U[/latex]'s diagonal, as [latex]U[/latex] is upper triangular), if [latex]P[/latex] is singular ([latex]\det(P)=0[/latex]) then [latex]\det(U)=0[/latex], which for a triangular matrix forces at least one diagonal entry to be [latex]0[/latex]. True.

If [latex]P[/latex] symmetric, both [latex]L,U[/latex] symmetric: plain LU decomposition does not generally preserve/reveal symmetry in [latex]L[/latex] and [latex]U[/latex] individually (that requires a specialized decomposition like [latex]LDL^T[/latex] or Cholesky). False in general.

Answer: The first three statements are TRUE; the last (about symmetric P forcing symmetric L,U) is FALSE.
